slides.narration: When two fractions share the same numerator, the denominator is the secret to which one is bigger. A bigger denominator means the whole has been cut into more pieces, so every single piece is smaller.
slides.caption: Same numerator, bigger denominator = smaller fraction
slides.imagePrompt: Two identical round pies on a wooden table side by side, the left pie cut into four equal slices and the right pie cut into eight equal slices, showing how the eight slices are noticeably thinner and smaller than the four slices

slides.narration: To find exactly where five eighths sits, you need to think carefully about what eighths look like compared to the whole. Picture the space between zero and one split into eight equal parts, and count five of those tiny steps from the start.
slides.caption: Five eighths: count five of eight equal steps
slides.imagePrompt: A long wooden fence stretching from left to right across a sunny meadow, the fence divided into eight perfectly equal sections by seven evenly spaced posts, with the first five sections painted bright yellow and the last three sections left plain brown

quiz.prompt: Place 5/8 on the number line. What percentage of the way from 0 to 1 is it?
quiz.explanation: 5 ÷ 8 = 0.625, which is 62.5% — closest reachable point on this slider is 65%. To find the position, divide the numerator by the denominator: 5 ÷ 8 = 0.625, so 5/8 sits just past the 60% mark.

slides.narration: When two fractions share the same denominator, the denominator is telling you the size of each piece — and that size never changes when you add. You only count up how many of those same-sized pieces you have altogether.
slides.caption: Same denominator? Only numerators add.
slides.imagePrompt: A round pie on a wooden table cut into eight perfectly equal slices, with three slices on one plate and four slices on a second plate beside it, a friendly hand gesturing toward both plates as if about to combine them

slides.narration: Look at the two plates — three eighths on one side and four eighths on the other. Count all the slices together and ask yourself: has the size of one slice changed at all? The bottom number stays eight, because every piece is still one eighth of the same pie.
slides.caption: Three eighths plus four eighths — count the pieces.
slides.imagePrompt: Two small plates each holding slices from the same eight-slice pie being slid together on a checkered tablecloth, all slices clearly identical in size, with an empty larger plate waiting to receive them all

quiz.explanation: When denominators match, add only the numerators: 3 + 4 = 7, and the denominator stays 8, giving 7/8. That fraction is already in simplest form since 7 and 8 share no common factors.

slides.narration: Here is something that will surprise you: a polar bear's fur is actually transparent, not white at all — it scatters light the way snow does, so it appears white against the Arctic ice. That one detail tells you something powerful about habitats, because every part of that bear's body was shaped by the place it lives. A habitat is not just a backdrop — it is a life-support system that must deliver four things: food, water, shelter, and space.
slides.caption: Four things every habitat must provide.
slides.imagePrompt: A massive polar bear standing on a sheet of Arctic sea ice surrounded by freezing blue ocean water, its thick fur blending into the snowy white landscape, a vast open sky above, photorealistic style.

slides.narration: Now think about what happens when even one of those four things disappears — say a forest loses its trees, or a wetland dries up. The animals that lived there cannot simply stay, because their bodies and behaviors were built for that exact place, not somewhere else. A polar bear cannot cool itself in a desert, and a cactus wren cannot survive a frozen tundra, because each animal fits its habitat the way a key fits a lock — perfectly, and only there.
slides.caption: Change the habitat, lose the animal.
slides.imagePrompt: A split scene showing a lush green wetland on one side full of herons wading in shallow water, and the same landscape on the other side cracked and dried to bare clay under a scorching sun with the birds gone, dramatic lighting emphasizing the contrast.

quiz.prompt: Each pair below names an animal and a habitat. Select the pairs where the habitat actually supplies all four survival needs for that animal.
quiz.explanation: A polar bear's Arctic habitat and a clownfish's coral reef each supply all four needs: food, water, shelter, and space. A camel's body is built for desert conditions — it cannot quickly adapt to a rainforest's humidity and different food sources, no matter how tough it is. An earthworm needs moist soil for oxygen exchange through its skin; submerged in pond water it would suffocate, so 'moist' and 'flooded' are not the same survival condition.

options: Polar bear — Arctic tundra, where sea ice provides hunting ground, fish and seals for food, and snow dens for shelter
Camel — tropical rainforest, because camels are tough and could adapt quickly if their desert was destroyed
Clownfish — coral reef, where the reef provides anemone shelter, plankton food, and warm salt water
Earthworm — freshwater pond, because earthworms prefer moist environments and a pond is very wet

slides.narration: The water cycle always begins with energy from the sun heating the surface of oceans, lakes, and rivers. That heat causes liquid water to escape into the air as an invisible gas called water vapor — this is evaporation, and it is always the engine that drives the whole cycle forward.
slides.caption: Sun's heat starts everything.
slides.imagePrompt: A brilliant sun blazing over a wide shimmering ocean, with faint wispy curls of vapor rising off the water surface into a pale blue sky

slides.narration: As water vapor floats higher into the sky, the air gets colder and the vapor clings together into tiny droplets, forming clouds — that process is called condensation, and it must happen before a single raindrop or snowflake can ever fall. Only after clouds have built up heavy with droplets does precipitation finally come down.
slides.caption: Vapor rises, clouds form first.
slides.imagePrompt: A dramatic scene showing puffy white clouds building high above green hills, with dark swollen rain clouds lower in the sky beginning to release streaks of rain onto the land below

quiz.prompt: A puddle sits in hot sunlight on a summer afternoon. Arrange these four stages in the order they happen next, one leading into the next.
quiz.explanation: Heat turns the puddle's water into vapor first — that's evaporation. The vapor rises, cools, and clumps into clouds through condensation before any rain can fall. Then precipitation brings water back down, and collection gathers it on the ground to start the cycle again.
